outlineItem.title: Chapter 1
outlineItem.text:
The centrifugal force of an otherwise hypnotically beautiful kaleidoscope melted Arch Stone's brain into a mass of pudding pooled against the sidewalls of his skull. Despite the G-forces applied to his circulatory system, Arch had enough neurons still firing to initiate the sequence for flat spin recovery. Throttle to idle. Stomp the right rudder to counter the leftward spin. Nose down.
“Fuuuuck meeeee!!!” Through clenched teeth, Stone grunted as he involuntarily constricted every muscle fiber in his 6'2“ frame.
The dizzying rotation intensified, forcing blood through irregular pathways in Stone's body, starving his brain of oxygen and depriving his senses of orientation. Static crept into his vision and like a computer powering down, his systems shut down systematically. Static vision went black, the pin pricks of blood restricted limbs dissipated into complete numbness, and finally, his all-consuming panic plunged into downy soft unconsciousness. Arch's subconscious was pillowed in memories, some recent, like the dinner with his fiancee Jessie on the Potomac dinner cruise; others distant, the rabid dog that gripped his pant leg during his hurried escape from a favela alley in São Paolo. He felt the sensation of the dog, pulling his leg, and steering his moped right, directly for a tree. No kicking, shouting, or thumping seemed to deter the beast in its parasitic quest to give the viral guest a pathway to continuation of life inside a new host. That would have been the case, no doubt, if not for the discarded paper sack that took the canine's steady traction away, slipping it's hind legs directly into the path of Arch's rear wheels. As sudden as the yelp, the unclenched jaws of the dog released the full power and agility of the moped. It quickly accelerated as Stone righted the machine, leaving the good-as-dead dog in a hopeless loop of trying to stand, failing, and trying again. Arch watched in the rear view as the poor beast, through no fault of its own, flailed and yelped--a tragic image permanently imprinted on his subconscious. The damp earth and hot wind from his memory gave way to the stench of pure ozone. The sensation of the sickly dog falling away from the moped blended into Arch's voluntary movements easing the rudders into stabilized flight. His senses returned, just as they had disappeared, one-by-one. Plainly visible horizon came into focus, though something was etched into the scene. Nothing like he had experienced in his 15-year command of aircraft. Six columns of anomalous atmosphere--three ahead, three behind--emmitted a soft amber glow. The incandescence just faint enough to make Arch wonder if his vision had truly returned. Light bent in random scattered waves through the the pillars in a violently churning mirage--a cursed spotlight beaming to the location of each of his comrades in formation. Except there was no longer a formation, all five planes vanished from the sky. Vaporized. Shortly after regaining control of his numb hands and feet, which still had the phantom sensations of his Brazilian moped vibrating through them, Arch's hearing returned with the familiar whip of air rapidly passing around his cockpit. Audibly missing were the buzzes and sirens he'd expect after nearly losing his aircraft. No master faults. No airspeed warnings. Nothing. Whatever it was took out the electronic avionics, but he still had control over the hydraulic surface controls. His analog altitude indicator told him that he breached the 10,000 foot mandatory ejection ceiling 2000 feet ago, as did the scenery below, passing by uncomfortably close. Arch pushed the throttle and turned to a heading of 208 degrees, what should be a straight shot back to Al Udeid. The bank angle gave Arch a clear view of spots of wreckage below. The scars in the earth below did not resemble the typical impact crater he expected. No black plumage of unspent fuel burning off. No charred earth. Simply a scorched wing here; a burnt vertical stabilizer there. The scene at the bottom of each column added to his confusion as he was unable to establish points of reference to determine an area of probability for search operations to locate, rescue, or return his fellow pilots. There were no indications of trajectory or points of impact. No sign that anyone ejected. Just bits of air frame scattered randomly across the Qatari desert floor.
“Skywings flight report,” The radio echoed disjointedly through unsynced speakers in Arch's helmet, “Do you read? Skywings flight report. Command is blind, what's going on out there.”
“Tower. Rockslide copy,” his arid vocals hitched, “Mayday, Skywings down. I don't know, all of them down. Mayday.”
“Rockslide, radar indicates 5 down, vector 2-3-0, report runway in sight, cleared for visual approach runway two-three. Field is clear. Do you need medical?”
“Wilco. Negative on medical.” Astonished by the energy required to communicate, Arch said a silent prayer for strength to bring his bird in for a landing.
“Copy. Maintain 2-3-0 at 3000. You're 8 miles northeast. Report visual on runway.”
“Wilco, 2-3-0 at three. Report runway. Rockslide.”
The jet's electronics came online, individually as if there was an invisible co-pilot flipping switches. Arch dialed heading 230 and 3000 feet into his avionics, sending the F-15EX on a southwest track home. His body eased back into the captains chair, sudden repose signaled by the ding indicating an engaged autopilot. As each system came online and the fighter jet's software performed its checks, the cockpit filled with inconsistent diagnoses for the aircraft. Master warnings directed Stone's focus to correct his electrical systems immediately while delaying remediations of amber warnings for cabin pressure, hydraulics, and icing sensors. Just like he had trained. Oddly, the voltage meter read normal on all sensors, generators all functioned nominally. Arch silenced the red master warning. The fault then reset and triggered the alarms again. Silenced, fault reset, fault tripped. In this sequence repeatedly, each initiation of alarms seemed to grow louder until the sounds evolved into a cacophony as if 100 overlaid recordings of a casino floor amplified through a loudspeaker pressurized his skull. Anxiety blanketed Arch's abilities to focus, make decisions, or think in general; the tighter the blanket wrapped, the more paralyzed he became. Archibald Stone, 35, United States Air Force Major, had been distilled into a skin sack filled with meat and blood. The only functioning reflexes were the autonomous control of a prefrontal cortex fine-tuned by decades of flight instruction. Breath continued in and out, his heart maintained rhythmic cycling of oxygen, and eyes nystagmically scanned the horizon for block letters, RW 23.

No kicking, shouting, or thumping seemed to deter the beast in its parasitic quest to give the viral guest a pathway to continuation of life inside a new host. That would have been the case, no doubt, if not for the discarded paper sack that took the canine's steady traction away, slipping it's hind legs directly into the path of Arch's rear wheels. As sudden as the yelp, the unclenched jaws of the dog released the full power and agility of the moped. It quickly accelerated as Stone righted the machine, leaving the good-as-dead dog in a hopeless loop of trying to stand, failing, and trying again. Arch watched in the rear view as the poor beast, through no fault of its own, flailed and yelped--a tragic image permanently imprinted on his subconscious. The damp earth and hot wind from his memory gave way to the stench of pure ozone. The sensation of the sickly dog falling away from the moped blended into Arch's voluntary movements easing the rudders into stabilized flight. His senses returned, just as they had disappeared, one-by-one. Plainly visible horizon came into focus, though something was etched into the scene. Nothing like he had experienced in his 15-year command of aircraft. Six columns of anomalous atmosphere, three ahead of him, three behind, emmitted a soft amber glow. The incandescence just faint enough to make Arch wonder if his vision had truly returned. Light bent in random scattered waves through the the pillars in a violently churning mirage--a cursed spotlight beaming to the location of each of his comrades in formation. Except there was no longer a formation, all five planes vanished from the sky. Vaporized. Shortly after regaining control of his numb hands and feet, which still had the phantom sensations of his Brazilian moped vibrating through them, Arch's hearing returned with the familiar whip of air rapidly passing around his cockpit. Audibly missing were the buzzes and sirens he'd expect after nearly losing his aircraft. No master faults. No airspeed warnings. Nothing. Whatever it was took out the electronic avionics, but he still had control over the hydraulic surface controls. His analog altitude indicator told him that he breached the 10,000 foot mandatory ejection ceiling 2000 feet ago, as did the scenery below, passing by uncomfortably close. Arch pushed the throttle and turned to a heading of 208 degrees, what should be a straight shot back to Al Udeid. The bank angle gave Arch a clear view of spots of wreckage below. The scars in the earth below did not resemble the typical impact crater he expected. No black plumage of unspent fuel burning off. No charred earth. Simply a scorched wing here; a burnt vertical stabilizer there. The scene at the bottom of each column added to his confusion as he was unable to establish points of reference to determine an area of probability for search operations to locate, rescue, or return his fellow pilots. There were no indications of trajectory or points of impact. No sign that anyone ejected. Just bits of air frame scattered randomly across the Qatari desert floor.
“Skywings flight report,” The radio echoed disjointedly through unsynced speakers in Arch's helmet, “Do you read? Skywings flight report. Command is blind, what's going on out there.”
“Tower. Rockslide copy,” his arid vocals hitched, “Mayday, Skywings down. I don't know, all of them down. Mayday.”
“Rockslide, radar indicates 5 down, vector 2-3-0, report runway in sight, cleared for visual approach runway two-three. Field is clear. Do you need medical?”
“Wilco. Negative on medical.” Astonished by the energy required to communicate, Arch said a silent prayer for strength to bring his bird in for a landing.
“Copy. Maintain 2-3-0 at 3000. You're 8 miles northeast. Report visual on runway.”
“Wilco, 2-3-0 at three. Report runway. Rockslide.”
The jet's electronics came online, individually as if there was an invisible co-pilot flipping switches. Arch dialed heading 230 and 3000 feet into his avionics, sending the F-15EX on a southwest track home. His body eased back into the captains chair, sudden repose signaled by the ding indicating an engaged autopilot. As each system came online and the fighter jet's software performed its checks, the cockpit filled with inconsistent diagnoses for the aircraft. Master warnings directed Stone's focus to correct his electrical systems immediately while delaying remediations of amber warnings for cabin pressure, hydraulics, and icing sensors. Just like he had trained. Oddly, the voltage meter read normal on all sensors, generators all functioned nominally. Arch silenced the red master warning. The fault then reset and triggered the alarms again. Silenced, fault reset, fault tripped. In this sequence repeatedly, each initiation of alarms seemed to grow louder until the sounds evolved into a cacophony as if 100 overlaid recordings of a casino floor amplified through a loudspeaker pressurized his skull. Anxiety blanketed Arch's abilities to focus, make decisions, or think in general; the tighter the blanket wrapped, the more paralyzed he became. Archibald Stone, 35-year-old, United States Air Force Major, had been distilled into a skin sack filled with meat and blood under the autonomous control of a prefrontal cortex. Breath continued in and out, heart maintained rhythmic cycling of oxygen, and for this USAF pilot, eyes nystagmically scanned the horizon for block letters, RW 23.
